# #005. Positive-Part Ramp & the Equality Trap

<!-- section:scenario -->
A thermal power unit operates across $T$ hours starting from `initialOutput`. In each hour $t \in \{0, \dots, T-1\}$, you choose generator output `outputs[t]` bounded by **`demands[t] <= outputs[t] <= maxOutput`** (excess power can be curtailed cleanly, so **meeting demand is an inequality `>=`, not `==`**).

Each hour incurs running cost `runCost * outputs[t]`, plus an asymmetric **startup/upward-ramping cost** `rampCost * max(0, outputs[t] - prevOutput)` where `prevOutput = initialOutput` for $t=0$ and `outputs[t-1]` for $t \ge 1$. Ramping **down** costs nothing. Minimize total cost!

<!-- section:io -->
- **Input (`P005Input`)**:
  - `demands: number[]` — minimum power required in each period $t$
  - `maxOutput: number` — turbine upper capacity
  - `initialOutput: number` — output level immediately prior to period $0$
  - `runCost: number` — per-MW running cost
  - `rampCost: number` — per-MW penalty on **positive increases** $(x_t - x_{t-1})_+$
- **Output (`P005Output`)**:
  - `outputs: number[]` — scheduled output per hour
  - `totalCost: number` — minimized running + upward ramping cost

<!-- section:example -->
Look carefully at Case 1: `demands = [180, 260, 120, 280]`, `runCost = 10`, `rampCost = 25`, `initialOutput = 100`.

- If you mistakenly force `outputs[t] == demands[t]`, period 2 drops to `120` MW and then pays `25 * (280 - 120) = 4,000` to ramp back up for a total of **`15,900`**.
- Instead, **staying hot** at `outputs = [180, 260, 260, 280]` generates `140` extra MW in hour 2 (costing `1,400`), saving `3,500` in ramp penalty — dropping total cost to **`14,300`**!

<!-- section:hint1 -->
Notice the asymmetry: we only pay when $x_t - x_{t-1} > 0$, using the **positive part** $(d)_+ = \max(0, d)$. Because the objective *minimizes* a positive multiple of $(x_t - x_{t-1})_+$, how can you represent $(d)_+$ with one non-negative auxiliary variable $u_t \ge 0$ and a single inequality?

<!-- section:hint2 -->
Introduce $u_t \ge 0$ (`lb: 0`) and enforce **`u[t] >= outputs[t] - prev`**!
- Why doesn't the opposite `outputs[t] - prev <= u[t]` accidentally let $u_t$ stay `0` when $d > 0$? It doesn't! Because `u[t] >= d` AND `u[t] >= 0` means `u[t] >= max(0, d)`, and minimizing cost pushes `u[t]` down onto `max(0, d)`.
- **Sign trap**: If you accidentally wrote `u[t] == outputs[t] - prev` or added `u[t] >= prev - outputs[t]`, you would charge for ramping down too (failing Case 2)!

<!-- section:formulation -->
$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x, u} \quad & \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \left( c_{\text{run}} x_t + c_{\text{ramp}} u_t \right) \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & d_t \le x_t \le X_{\max} && \forall t \\
& u_t \ge x_t - x_{t-1} && \forall t \;\; (x_{-1} = x_{\text{init}}) \\
& u_t \ge 0 && \forall t
\end{aligned}
$$

Two classic LP traps live here: confusing **`==` with `>=`** on demand (cutting off economical valley holding), and adding symmetric absolute-value bounds when only one sign (`+` vs `-`) is penalized!
